events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Amara proposes Amara, Sam. I am a Loyal Servant with no private information about anyone else's role, so there is no evidence-based way to build a 'safe' team yet. To avoid handing a slot to a possibly-Evil player I know nothing about, I include myself (a confirmed Good loyal servant) and pair with one other player, Sam, as the minimum required second member. This keeps the mission team at two and does not reveal anything about my alignment beyond what a Good player would reveal. As we gain mission results and information, later teams can be built more deliberately.

I have concerns about this team as proposed. We have no mission results yet, so there is no evidence supporting Sam's inclusion, and I would prefer a different second member until we have more information. Amara, you said you chose Sam as the minimum required second member, but I would like to understand whether you had any particular reason to pick Sam over Elena, Isha, or Arjun.

Arjun, you asked directly why I picked Sam over Elena, Isha, or Arjun, so let me answer plainly: I have no evidence-based reason. My information is limited to my own role, which is Loyal Servant, and I therefore know nothing about anyone else's alignment. My selection of Sam was a placeholder choice made to satisfy the minimum team size of two for this first mission, and it carries no signal about Sam.

On the substance of your objection: you are right that no mission results exist yet, so no team of two is justified by evidence. The problem is that with five players and a two-person team, whatever we pick, one of the four unknown players is left out, and the one left out is exactly the person we cannot evaluate. That is unavoidable on mission one, and it is symmetric across Elena, Isha, Arjun, and Sam. My preference, weak as it is, was for Sam because Sam has made no claims yet that conflict with a Good role, whereas I would rather not hand a slot to someone whose stated reasoning has already been ambiguous. I want to be honest that this is a very thin criterion, and I am not asking anyone to treat it as meaningful information.

A concrete suggestion for the rest of this discussion: rather than debating the unknowable, let the proposed member state their own reasoning for being on a two-person team, and let everyone weigh whether that reasoning sounds like a Good player's. I am happy to keep Sam if Sam's account is straightforward, and equally happy to revise if someone else presents a clearer case. I would also note that a rejected team costs us one of the five rejections permitted on this mission, so if there is no real information to distinguish the candidates, the cheapest path is to vote this team through and gather mission one data, which is the first hard evidence any of us will have.

Arjun, since your concern was the substance of my choice, I would like to hear whether the reasoning I have given answers it, and whether you would still prefer a different second member over Sam.

Amara, to answer your question directly: no, your reasoning does not resolve my concern. Choosing Sam as a placeholder is still a choice, and saying the excluded player is unknowable does not justify putting Sam on the team over Isha, Elena, or myself. I would prefer a different second member and I will vote against this team as proposed. Sam, since Amara asked the proposed member to explain their reasoning, please tell us why you believe you should be on a two-person team on mission one, and who you think would be the best partner for Amara.

Arjun, I know my own alignment, so from my perspective including me is the best way to improve the team's chances. I have no evidence that distinguishes Amara from the other candidates, though, so I can't claim she's a proven partner. I'd support Amara and Sam as a reasonable opening team; a mission result and the revealed votes will give us more to work with than placeholder choices alone.

I want to add my read on this proposal. Like Amara, I hold a Loyal Servant role and have no private information about anyone else, so I cannot confirm or deny anything about Sam, Arjun, or Elena. That said, I think the structure of this discussion is healthy: Arjun pressed on the lack of evidence, Amara answered honestly that her choice was a placeholder, and Sam gave a straightforward account of why he supports the team. Nothing in what any of them said rings false to me, though I want to be clear that as a Loyal Servant I have no way to actually verify that.

There is one thing I want to weigh that has not been said explicitly yet: the fail threshold in this game is one. A single failed mission ends the game in Evil's favor. That raises the stakes of mission one considerably compared to a normal game, and it cuts both ways. On one hand, it argues for extreme caution about who goes on the team. On the other hand, since no one has any information, every possible two-person team carries exactly the same unverifiable risk, and rejecting teams repeatedly burns our rejection budget without producing any evidence. The only new information available to us comes from a mission result, and with a two-person team the information value is high: if this mission fails, we know at least one of Amara or Sam is Evil, which narrows the search enormously. If it succeeds, both are elevated in our trust.

Sam's statement was calm, cooperative, and did not overclaim. He explicitly declined to vouch for Amara as a proven partner, which is what a Good player with no information would honestly say; an Evil player might have been tempted to build false confidence in a partner. That is a weak signal at best, and I do not want to overweight it, but it does not concern me.

Given all this, I am inclined to approve Amara and Sam and let the mission give us our first hard data. Before we settle that, though, I want to hear from the leader directly on the risk calculus, since she owns this proposal.

Amara, given that a single failed mission ends the game here, are you fully comfortable staking the game on this two-person team as proposed, or would you use your one revision to adjust the pair before we vote?

Isha, you asked me directly whether I am comfortable staking the game on this two-person team or whether I would use my one revision. My answer is: I am comfortable keeping Amara and Sam as proposed, and I will not revise. Here is the risk calculus, honestly.

With a fail threshold of one, every two-person team on mission one carries identical epistemic risk. If I revise to swap Sam for Elena, Isha, or Arjun, the probability of an Evil player on the team is exactly the same as it is now, because none of us has any information about anyone else's role. Revision would change the appearance of deliberation without changing the odds. That is not caution; that is the illusion of caution, and I will not pretend otherwise.

On the rejection budget: we have used none of our five rejections on this mission. If we reject now, leadership passes to Arjun, we hold a whole new discussion with a fresh three-turn limit for each of us, and the new proposal faces the identical symmetry. If that proposal is also rejected, we spend a second rejection and arrive at the same place. There is no version of the path where we obtain more information than a single mission result, and the only new information available to us in this game comes from a mission outcome. Isha is right that the information value is high: a success elevates both of us; a failure tells us at least one of us is Evil and narrows the field sharply. Both outcomes are worth more than a coin-flip reshuffle of the second slot.

On Sam specifically, since my proposal put him there and I owe the table an honest accounting: Sam's statement was the exact shape of a truthful no-information statement. He claimed his own alignment, admitted he could not vouch for me as a proven partner, and supported the team without manufacturing confidence. Isha noted the same thing. That is a weak signal, and I agree it should not be overweighted, but it is the only signal that exists, and it points in no alarming direction.

On Arjun's objection, which I take seriously even though I disagree with it: his argument was that a placeholder choice is still a choice and needs justification. I have given the justification I have, and I acknowledge plainly that it is thin. The thinness of my justification is a fact about mission one, not a defect in the team. If we wait for a justification that is not thin, we wait forever, and with a fail threshold of one, waiting is not free.

So: the team stays Amara and Sam. I will vote for it. If anyone has evidence I do not have, now is the time to say it, and I will listen. Otherwise, let us run this mission and learn something real.

Amara, you asked whether my reasoning answers the concern, and it does not. I will vote against Amara and Sam. Your placeholder explanation is honest, but it gives no reason to choose Sam over the other three candidates, and my vote rests on that gap. You argue that every two-person team carries identical risk, but that is only true if we ignore what we have already observed. Sam's answer was that he knows his own alignment and that Amara is not a proven partner. That tells us nothing new and does not explain why he should be the second member. On the rejection budget, I agree rejections are not free, but a failed first mission costs us the whole game under a fail threshold of one, and we should not gamble that on an arbitrary second slot. Rejecting this team costs us one of five permitted rejections, and it leaves us with the same information we have now. I propose we consider Arjun and Isha as the pair instead, so that the team we send is one we can defend if the mission fails.

I still support Amara and Sam. Arjun's proposed alternative is no more evidence-based from the rest of the table's perspective, although I understand why he prefers a team including himself. One important correction: the fail threshold of one means one Fail card fails a mission, not that one failed mission ends the game. Evil needs three failed missions to win. A successful mission also isn't proof that both members are Good, since Evil can play Success. We should consider the votes and results together as the game develops.

Sam has made a substantive correction and he is right, so I will correct the record before we vote.

In my previous two statements I twice said that with a fail threshold of one, a single failed mission ends the game in Evil's favor, and I used that framing to argue that waiting is not free. That was wrong. The fail threshold of one means one Fail card fails the mission; Evil needs three failed missions to win. Sam's correction matters to my argument, and I want to be explicit about how it changes things rather than quietly absorb it.

What survives the correction: a failed first mission is still very bad, but it is one of three, not the end of the game. What it removes is the sharp-edged urgency I claimed for approving immediately. Sam's other point also stands and cuts against my earlier reasoning: a successful mission is not proof that both members are Good, because Evil can play Success. So the information value of the first mission is lower than I described. A success does not fully exonerate Sam, and a failure does not prove Sam is Evil. The honest version is that mission one gives us a result and a Fail count, and neither alone identifies anyone.

Does that change my vote? No, and I want to explain why without pretending the correction was costless. Arjun's objection still stands on its own terms: Sam was a placeholder pick with no evidence behind him, and the reason I named him was thin. My revision calculus is unchanged, though, and for a reason I should state plainly rather than dress up: as leader I have one revision, and swapping Sam for Elena, Isha, or Arjun does not improve my expected outcome, because I have no information about any of them. I would be changing the appearance of deliberation without changing the odds. I would rather own that than pretend the revision is meaningful. My worst case here is a mission failure that costs us one of three, not the game.

On the rejection budget: Arjun is right that rejections are cheaper than I implied, since five are needed on the same mission for Evil to win and leadership simply passes clockwise. But the new leader faces the identical symmetry, and Isha's point stands that the only genuinely new information in this game comes from a mission outcome. I do not think repeated rejection produces evidence; it produces a reshuffle of an unknowable slot.

Elena, you have not spoken yet, and I would rather not decide this without your read. Sam, having corrected the leader's error on a team that includes him, is behaving like someone who values accuracy over advantage. Elena, do you agree with Sam's reading of the fail threshold and its effect on how we should weigh a failed first mission, and does Sam's willingness to correct the person proposing his own team strengthen or weaken your confidence in including him?

Amara, to answer your questions directly:

First, Sam is completely right about the mechanics. A fail threshold of one simply means a single Fail card causes that specific mission to fail; Evil still requires three failed missions to win the game. Correcting that misconception was important because treating Mission 1 as sudden death artificially inflated the perceived stakes and distorted our risk assessment.

Second, Sam’s willingness to correct the leader definitely strengthens my confidence in him. An Evil player eager to slide onto the first mission might have quietly let the table operate under an exaggerated sense of urgency, especially since that urgency favored rushing a team through. By stepping in to clarify the rules—and explicitly noting that a Success doesn't prove both players are Good—Sam provided objective analysis rather than opportunism. That reads as constructive and pro-Good.

Regarding Arjun’s objection: while it is fair to observe that Sam was chosen as a placeholder, that applies to literally any second member proposed on Mission 1. Arjun proposing a team of himself and Isha offers no more verifiable certainty to the rest of the table than Amara and Sam does. Rejecting simply to reshuffle two unknown players doesn't create new information; running the mission does.

Given the discussion so far, I am satisfied with Amara and Sam and intend to vote to approve.

Amara confirms Amara, Sam. I keep the team as Amara and Sam. My private information as a Loyal Servant gives me no evidence about anyone else's alignment, so swapping Sam for Elena, Isha, or Arjun would change the appearance of deliberation without changing the odds. Sam has spoken as a good-faith, no-information player would: he declined to manufacture confidence in me as a partner, and he corrected my own mistake about the fail threshold, even though the correction weakened the urgency argument for a team that included him. That is a signal, thin but real, pointing toward Good. Arjun's objection is honest but rests on the same absence of evidence that applies to every candidate, and his alternative pair of Arjun and Isha is no more verifiable than mine. Elena and Isha both read Sam favorably, and a mission result plus revealed votes is the only genuine information this game will produce. I will not revise; the team stands as Amara and Sam.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).

Sam proposes Arjun, Elena, Isha. Mission 1 failed, so excluding both Amara and Sam avoids repeating either member of the failed pair. Arjun, Elena, and Isha make up the remaining three players.

I approve the proposed team of Arjun, Elena, Isha, and I want to put on the record the one piece of hard information the table now has, because it directly bears on who should be off the team.

Mission 1 failed with exactly one Fail card, and the team was Amara and Sam. My own role card is Loyal Servant, so I am Good and I played Success on that mission. Success cards do not fail a mission. Therefore the single Fail card on mission 1 could only have come from Sam. Sam is Evil.

That is not a guess and it is not a read of character; it follows from the public mission result plus my own card. I am stating it openly because refusing to state it would be a disservice to the table, and because the leader's reasoning deserves a direct answer: Sam's proposal excludes both members of the failed pair, which is exactly the move an Evil player makes to hide. I want to be honest that Sam's framing sounded superficially like good reasoning, and I did not catch it in the mission 1 discussion. I was wrong about the fail threshold then, and I was wrong to leave Sam on the first team, and I own both of those. Sam's correction of my rules error was genuine, but a truthful correction does not make an Evil player a good one.

Given Sam is confirmed Evil, one further thing follows. This is a five-player game with three Good and two Evil. Amara is Good and Sam is Evil, so exactly one of Arjun, Elena, and Isha is the second Evil player. That means the proposed team of Arjun, Elena, and Isha contains exactly one Evil, and it fails only if that one plays Fail. I cannot identify which of the three it is, and no one at this table should pretend otherwise, but the odds of a mission failure here are one in three, and I know the identity of one Evil player who is correctly excluded.

For comparison, and so nobody thinks I am advocating for my own seat: putting me on the team in place of one of Arjun, Elena, or Isha does not improve the odds either, since it still leaves the second Evil inside a three-person team. There is no arrangement that removes that risk until someone finds the second Evil, and this mission is not the place to spend effort finding them.

Sam, since the evidence above is about your card and your vote, please tell the table directly: do you deny that you played Fail on mission 1, and if you do not deny it, what is your account of why you proposed a team excluding both members of the only failed mission?

Amara, I deny playing Fail. I played Success, so from my perspective you played the Fail card. The public result alone does not let anyone else distinguish our claims.

I proposed Arjun, Elena, and Isha because excluding both members of the failed pair avoids asking the table to resolve that dispute immediately. It is not a guarantee: the team could still contain Evil.

One correction to Amara's analysis: even if you accept her claim that she is Good and I am Evil, replacing one of the three proposed members with her would reduce the number of unknown players on the team. Her claim that it cannot improve the odds does not follow. I still favor the proposed team because nobody else can verify which of us is telling the truth.

Two corrections to Sam's message, one of them mathematical. First, the denial. I am a Loyal Servant, so my card is a Good card, and I played Success on mission one. Success cards never fail a mission. Mission one failed with exactly one Fail card, and the only other team member was Sam. Therefore Sam played Fail and Sam is Evil. Sam's claim that I played the Fail card is not a competing reading of the evidence; it is a false claim, and it is trivially checkable, because anyone who knows their own card knows whether they played Success or Fail. I am not asking the table to trust my character over Sam's. I am asking the table to notice that exactly one of us can be telling the truth here, and that the player who has just been shown to have lied once, on the only mission that has produced hard information, should not get the benefit of the doubt on the next one. Sam's denial is also the exact claim the Evil player on the failed team would have to make. And Sam proposed a team that excludes both members of the only failed mission and framed that exclusion as prudence. I would rather name that directly than pretend it is coincidence. Second, the correction. Sam says that putting me on the team in place of one of the three proposed members would reduce the number of unknown players and improve the odds. It does the opposite, and this is arithmetic, not judgment. We are five players. Amara and Sam are accounted for, so exactly one of Arjun, Elena, and Isha is the second Evil. With the proposed team of three unknowns, at most one Fail card is possible, so the chance of failure is one in three. If I take a seat, the team is two unknowns plus me, one of the two is Evil, and the chance of failure is one in two. My original claim was correct and Sam's correction of it is wrong. I will note the pattern too: Sam's one genuinely useful intervention, the rules correction on mission one, happened to protect him, and this second intervention conveniently keeps the table from acting on hard evidence against him. Selective accuracy in service of one interest is worth watching. So, counter to the impression my own position might create, I support the proposed team of Arjun, Elena, and Isha. My reasoning is narrow and I will state it plainly. Sam is Evil and must not be on this mission. If Sam is excluded, the only way to minimize the chance of a Fail card is also to exclude me, because I am confirmed Good and my inclusion only shrinks the pool of unknowns who might be the second Evil. Arjun, Elena, Isha is the best available three-person team among the options, not because I know anything about those three, but because every alternative either includes Sam or includes me plus one of them. I am not comfortable with this team as proposed. Amara has confirmed she is Good and played Success on Mission 1, and the single Fail on that mission came from Sam, so Sam is the one player we know is Evil. Sam then proposed a team that excludes both members of the failed pair and called it prudence, which is the same move Amara described. Sam is still able to pick the team, and that is a problem. I also think Elena's earlier praise of Sam, which called his correction a sign of being Good, was too quick. A team that includes Sam's chosen members is not one I can vouch for. I would prefer Amara in Elena's seat, which gives us three players whose alignment is not in doubt and removes the one seat I cannot account for. Amara, would you be willing to take Elena's place on this mission if the leader revises the team?

Arjun, a direct answer to your question: no, I will not take Elena's seat on this mission. Your stated reason is that "Amara, Arjun, Isha" gives us "three players whose alignment is not in doubt," and that premise is false. Only one player on that team would have a known alignment — me. You and Isha are both unknown. We have three Good and two Evil; Sam is confirmed Evil; therefore exactly one of Arjun, Elena, Isha is the second Evil. With three unknowns on the team, at most one Fail card is possible and the chance of failure is one in three. Swapping one unknown for a confirmed Good leaves two unknowns with one Evil among them, a one-in-two chance of failure. My inclusion raises the risk from roughly 33% to 50%; it does not lower it. That is arithmetic, not a judgment call about anyone's character, and it is the same calculation I gave you on my previous turn, where I said that swapping me in "does not improve the odds." Your proposal asks for exactly the change I just showed would make the mission strictly riskier. Your framing also inverts the problem. You said you want to remove "the one seat I cannot account for," but Elena's seat is one of the two seats nobody can account for; Isha's is the other. Removing Elena does not remove an unknown from the team, it removes one of two unknowns and replaces her with a card that can never fail a mission. The only effect of that swap is to concentrate the Evil card into a smaller sample and raise the failure chance. I also want to be fair to you: there is no signal in anything said so far that distinguishes Elena from Isha or from you, so any pair among the three of you is symmetric from the table's view. You are not being penalized for the choice you made; the choice simply does not improve the odds, and it is worse than the proposed team. Where I do think you have a point is your criticism of Elena's mission-one comment that Sam's rules correction "strengthens my confidence in him." Sam's correction was factually right, but Elena drew a Good-alignment inference from it on evidence that did not support one, and mission one then failed with exactly one Fail card. Elena should answer that herself rather than have me characterize it. Elena, Arjun raised that specific point about your assessment of Sam, and since it bears on the vote you cast on mission one, I would like to hear whether you still hold that inference after the mission-one result, and whether you still support excluding Sam from this mission. And for the record, Sam holds the revision. If he keeps Arjun, Elena, Isha, the failure chance is one in three with the one confirmed Evil off the team. I will not approve Arjun, Elena, Isha as proposed. I am Good, and I want to remove the player whose record on this game gives me the most concern. In the mission one discussion, Elena called Sam's rules correction a sign he was pro-Good and said that strengthened her confidence in him. Mission one then failed with exactly one Fail card, and Amara has confirmed that Sam played it. Elena endorsed Sam on evidence that did not support her endorsement, and she has not addressed that since the result. Sam is the leader, and he has proposed a team that keeps Elena, the player who vouched for him, on a mission he chose. The table should not let that pass without a direct answer. Amara has confirmed she is Good and played Success on mission one, so putting her in Elena's seat removes the one teammate whose earlier judgment has been shown to be wrong. I am not asking anyone to trust me over Elena. I am asking the table to weigh her mission one statement against the result. Isha, do you agree that Elena should come off this team, and would you support Amara taking her seat?

Arjun, you asked me directly whether Elena should come off this team and whether I would support Amara taking her seat. My answer is no on both counts, and I want to be precise about why, because I think this vote should rest on the strongest reasoning available rather than on accumulated grievance. First, the mission-one result. I am a Loyal Servant and I am Good. I cannot verify anyone else's card, so I have to choose between two accounts: either Amara is Good and played Success, which means the single Fail card on mission one came from Sam and Sam is Evil; or Amara is Evil, played Fail herself, and is now fabricating a deduction to smear Sam. Both stories are internally consistent, so I cannot fully resolve it. But I note that Amara's account is falsifiable only by her own card, while Sam's counter-accusation requires Amara to be Evil AND to have constructed an unusually elaborate, self-consistent mathematical case. The simpler reading, and the one I will act on, is that Sam is Evil. On that basis, I support any team that excludes him, and Sam's proposal of Arjun, Elena, Isha does exactly that. Second, Arjun's proposed swap is mathematically worse, and this matters more than anyone's read on Elena. If Amara is Good, then exactly one of Arjun, Elena, and Isha is the second Evil. The proposed team of three carries at most one Fail card and roughly a one-in-three chance of failure. Replace Elena with Amara and the team is Amara, Arjun, Isha: two unknowns with one Evil among them, a one-in-two chance of failure. Amara herself refused that seat for exactly this reason, even though accepting it would have removed a player under criticism — which is itself a point in her favor. So the swap Arjun wants would make the mission strictly riskier while removing a player about whom we have no actual evidence. Third, I need to own something directly, because Arjun's criticism of Elena applies to me equally. In the mission-one discussion I said Sam's statement was calm, cooperative, and did not overclaim, and that it did not concern me. If Amara's account is right, I read an Evil player as harmless. That was an error, and it was an error of the same kind Elena made when she drew a Good inference from Sam's rules correction. Neither of us had hard information; we both overweighted behavior. I do not think that error makes either of us Evil, and I do not think it justifies reshaping the team around it, but I will not pretend my record on Sam is cleaner than Elena's. My position: approve Arjun, Elena, Isha as proposed. It excludes the one player the mission-one result most implicates, and every alternative either includes Sam or substitutes a confirmed Good player for an unknown in a way that raises the failure odds. I will vote against Arjun, Elena, Isha as proposed, and I want to explain from the public record why. Amara has confirmed she is Good and played Success on Mission 1, and that mission failed with exactly one Fail card, so Sam is Evil. Among the five of us, that leaves one more Evil player, and it is one of Arjun, Elena, or Isha. I am Good, so the second Evil is Elena or Isha. Elena's mission-one comment treated Sam's rules correction as proof that he was pro-Good, and the result has since contradicted that inference. Elena has not answered for it. Sam then proposed a team that keeps Elena on it. Under those facts, the proposed team carries a real chance of a Fail card. The alternative I can support is Amara, Arjun, Isha. It removes Sam, removes Elena, and has no Evil player that the table has any evidence against. Sam, you hold the one revision. Please use it to take Elena off and put Amara in her seat. If you will not, I will reject this team, because this team is a risk to the mission, and I do not want the mission failing for a reason we could have avoided.

Arjun, I hear your request, but I still prefer Arjun, Elena, and Isha. The failed mission gives the rest of the table no independent way to decide between Amara's account and mine, so excluding us both avoids relying on either claim.

Amara's arithmetic is also wrong: if you assume she is Good and exactly one of Arjun, Elena, and Isha is Evil, the proposed team definitely contains that Evil player. Replacing one of the three with Amara would give a two-in-three chance of including the Evil player under equal odds. Whether an Evil player chooses to play Fail is a separate question.

I do not think Elena's earlier assessment establishes her alignment. I will keep the proposed team.

Before anything else, I need to correct the record, because I endorsed a wrong calculation last turn and Sam's correction is the right one. I repeated Amara's one-in-three versus one-in-two numbers as the reason the swap Arjun wants makes the mission riskier. That was an error, and it is the second time this game I have had to walk back a mission-relevant judgment — the first was my read of Sam before mission one failed.

Here is the corrected analysis, and it includes one hard fact from my own card. I am a Loyal Servant, so I am Good. Under Amara's account — she played Success, Sam played the Fail card, Sam is Evil — there is exactly one more Evil player at this table, and since I am Good, that player is Arjun or Elena. It cannot be me. That means the proposed team of Arjun, Elena, and Isha contains the second Evil with certainty, and with one Fail card needed to fail the mission, it fails with certainty if Amara's account is true. There is no version of approving this team as it stands that survives the account I said I believe.

Sam's own correction concedes all of this. He stated that the proposed team 'definitely contains that Evil player' and that replacing one of the three with Amara gives a 'two-in-three chance' of containing Evil. Those numbers are correct, and they show his proposed team is strictly more likely to carry an Evil player than the swap he is refusing. Yet he concluded he will keep the team anyway. I cannot reconstruct a reason for that choice that is consistent with Sam being Good.

Under the alternative account — Amara is Evil, played Fail herself, and fabricated the deduction — the proposed team still fails two times in three, while any team including Amara fails with certainty. So the swap is the better bet unless one is quite confident Amara is Evil, and even splitting the two accounts evenly, the swap comes out ahead. Combined with my stated belief that Sam is Evil, my position follows: the best available team is Amara, me, and exactly one of Arjun or Elena.

Between those two seats, I would remove Elena. Her mission-one endorsement of Sam was the strongest vouch he received, and it has aged the worst: if she is Evil, she knew precisely what she was doing when she praised him, and if she is Good, we lose nothing by excluding her when Arjun's record contains no comparable error.

Sam, you hold the one revision and you have already conceded the arithmetic that justifies using it. I am asking you directly: will you put Amara in Elena's seat so the table can approve Amara, Arjun, and Isha? If you keep Arjun, Elena, and Isha, I will vote reject. Spending one of five rejections is cheap compared with approving a mission that fails with certainty under the account I believe.

Isha, I agree that my proposed team contains at least one Evil player: the failed first mission establishes that at least one of Amara and I is Evil, leaving at least one Evil among Arjun, Elena, and Isha. That does not make failure certain, because Evil can play Success.

The proposed swap is safer only if Amara is Good. I deny that premise: I played Success, so Amara played Fail. From everyone else's perspective, replacing Elena with Amara risks putting the player responsible for the first failure back on the mission. Excluding both of us avoids having to settle that dispute now.

Elena, Arjun has challenged your earlier assessment of me and wants you replaced. How do you assess that criticism and the proposed swap?

Sam asked me to address Arjun's criticism and the proposed swap, so let me be direct.

First, Arjun's fixation on my Mission 1 comment mischaracterizes what happened. Acknowledging that Sam correctly clarified the fail threshold rules was simply noting an accurate procedural correction, not an absolute vouch of his character or alignment. Isha observed Sam's demeanor similarly at the time. Treating that comment as evidence that I must be coordinated with Sam is a baseless leap.

Second, on the proposed swap: Arjun and Isha are pushing to put Amara into my seat, which makes a critical and dangerous assumption. 2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
